claims.evidence: CMO guidance sources (healthcheck.nhs.uk CMO summary, NHS alcohol units page): not regularly more than 14 units a week, spread over three days or more.
As c01.

Sources say there is no fully safe level and 14 units is low risk, not safe; the 'because no level improves health' reasoning was not found and the CMO report accepts some small protective effect in some groups.
claims.newSentence: The guidance says there is no completely safe level of regular drinking; 14 units a week is described as a low-risk level, not a safe one.

claims.evidence: NHS Alcohol units page: one unit = 10ml or 8g pure alcohol; ABV is on labels and used in the unit formula.
CMO pregnancy advice (2016): no level is safe; safest not to drink at all. Search summaries state this.
As c01.
CMO/NHS: if you drink as much as 14 units, spread over three or more days.
See c03: 'no definitively safe lower limit because no level improves health' not confirmed as worded.
claims.newSentence: The guidance also says there is no completely safe level of regular drinking, so 14 units is a way to keep risk low rather than a safe amount.

claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales gives the weekly figure only; a Cornwall NHS leaflet still quotes 2-3 units a day; CMO chose a weekly limit.
NHS Alcohol units: 10ml or 8g pure alcohol per unit.
NHS Alcohol units: ABV is the percentage of pure alcohol by volume, printed on labels.
NHS Alcohol units: volume (ml) x ABV divided by 1,000.
NHS Alcohol units: 568ml of 5.2% lager = 2.95, about 3 units.

Drinkaware: 14 units is about six pints of 4% beer or six 175ml glasses of 13% wine; Alcohol Change says six pints of normal-strength beer (wine described differently, so 'average-strength' is acceptable but check).

Retrieved: alcohol is a risk factor for seven cancers (Alcohol Change) and raises risk of death from long-term illnesses and accidents (CMO). Heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes and mental health problems were not seen in returned text.
claims.newSentence: The Chief Medical Officers' guidance says regular drinking above the low-risk level raises the risk of dying from long-term illnesses and from accidents and injuries, and alcohol is a risk factor for seven types of cancer.

claims.evidence: Accidents and injuries confirmed; alcohol poisoning and violence/abuse as named short-term risks in the guidance were not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: The guidance also names accidents and injuries among the short-term risks of heavy drinking.

claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales alcohol poisoning/alcohol page: considerable risk of alcohol poisoning when drinking many units over a short period.

UK gov oral cancer toolkit: risk of mouth cancer rises with any alcohol or tobacco use; review (NCBI PMC6527045) says combined effect multiplicative. Ledger URL (Drinkaware guideline page) not shown to carry it.
Expert group summary (gov.uk): lifetime risk of dying from an alcohol-related condition around or a little under 1% at the low-risk level (search wording 'at or above').
Alcohol Change/CMO: risk rises with amount drunk.
gov.uk news/CMO: 14 units is a low-risk threshold, not a safe one.
As c05.

Alcohol Change 'Am I drinking too much' lists drinking more over time, struggling to cut down, poor sleep, thinking about next drink; NHS adds others being concerned. Ledger URL (Drinkaware guideline page) not shown to carry it.
NHS Better Health drink-less page: Drinkline 0300 123 1110, free, confidential, for anyone worried about their own or another's drinking.
Better Health: NHS Drink Free Days app lets users plan alcohol-free days and set a weekly unit target.
NHS guidance suggests a daily note of drinks, time, place and units; page carrying it among returned results not identified precisely.
Alcohol-free days (CMO) and lower-strength drinks / alternating with soft drinks (NHS) confirmed; eating before drinking and diluting drinks not found.
claims.newSentence: Having several alcohol-free days each week is another suggestion, as are choosing lower-strength drinks and alternating alcoholic drinks with soft drinks.

claims.evidence: Alcohol-use disorder - NHS: treatment from a GP or specialist alcohol addiction service.
NHS: counselling, self-help/mutual aid groups, talking therapies such as CBT, medicines (acamprosate, naltrexone).
AA and SMART Recovery named as mutual aid groups; Al-Anon Family Groups is support for families and friends, not a group for the person drinking.
claims.newSentence: Alcoholics Anonymous and SMART Recovery are named as self-help groups, and Al-Anon Family Groups as support for families and friends of people who drink.

claims.evidence: NHS: if not ready to stop or only want to cut down, you will be supported to reduce drinking to a safer level.

NHS says stopping suddenly can be very dangerous if dependent and to get medical help first. NHS England: severe symptoms (confusion, hallucinations, seizure) mean 999/A&E. NHS Scotland: 111 for confusion, hallucinations, severe anxiety, seizures. Shakes and sweats are common symptoms, not the stated trigger; the draft implies 111 for them and omits 999 for seizures. Also rests on one local leaflet.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says it can be very dangerous to stop drinking suddenly for someone who is dependent on alcohol, and that anyone who gets withdrawal symptoms should get medical help before trying to stop; for severe symptoms such as confusion, hallucinations or a seizure it advises calling 999 or going to A&E.

notes: Used 10 searches. Drinkaware low-risk page itself was returned but its text was blended with CMO sources; CMO claims are supported by gov.uk/NHS summaries. c14 wine equivalent differs between sources (Drinkaware 175ml of 13% vs Alcohol Change 1.5 bottles). c32 is the safety-critical fix: withdrawal urgency needs 999 for seizures, and shakes/sweats alone are not the stated trigger. c26 and c32 page attribution is partly inferred from blended summaries; the Scottish NHS Borders leaflet itself was not confirmed.
